chunks: Switching frequency upper and lower limits. The question: What limits the switching frequency on the upper and lower ends? Why can't the switching frequency be 1THz or 1 hertz?
A buck's switching frequency cannot be pushed arbitrarily high or low.
At the high end, every cycle wastes a bit of energy and the switches cannot make pulses shorter than a minimum time.
At the low end, the inductor and capacitor must grow huge to hold the same ripple. The usable range sits between those walls.
Think of a drummer keeping a steady beat. A stick can only bounce so fast, and each hit costs some effort, so tapping faster and faster eventually fails.
Tap very slowly and each hit has to be enormous to keep the sound continuous.
A buck is the same: too fast and the switches cannot keep up, too slow and the inductor and capacitor must absorb enormous swings.
The loss grows linearly, a straight line on log-log axes with slope 1. It crosses 1 watts at about 3. 7 megahertz for this device set, already more than the whole loss budget a 6.
6 watts converter can usually afford (about 0. 5 watts).
At 1 THz the formula gives 270 kilowatts, but the physics fails long before: edges take nanoseconds, longer than the period.
Better devices (GaN) lower the energy per cycle and move the crossing out by an order of magnitude.
Switching frequency ( f sw ): switching cycles per second. Minimum on-time: the shortest pulse the switch and driver can reliably make.
Switching loss: energy lost each cycle, so total loss grows with f sw ("Switching frequency vs efficiency and ripple").
Duty cycle ( D ): the fraction of each cycle the top switch is on ("What is duty cycle").
Crossover frequency: how fast the control loop can respond; it must stay well below f sw .
Convert 12 volts to 1. 2 volts, so D equals 0. 1 . Say the controller cannot make pulses shorter than 50 nanoseconds.
The switch is on for the fraction D of each period, and a period lasts 1 over f , so the on-time is D over f .
It must be at least 50 nanoseconds, so f at most D over t on min equals 0. 1 over 50 nanoseconds equals 2 megahertz. Above that, the output would not regulate correctly.
At the low end, inductance goes as 1 over f , so a 10 times lower frequency needs about a 10 times bigger inductor. That is the whole idea.
